claim: CHP3 is an EF-hand Ca2+-binding protein involved in regulation of cancerogenesis, cardiac hypertrophy, and neuronal development through interactions with sodium/proton exchangers (NHEs) and signalling proteins.
source: Calcineurin B homologous protein 3 (CHP3, tescalcin) belongs to the EF-hand Ca2+-binding protein (EFCaBP) family (Kolobynina et al., 2016) and is closely related to calcineurin B homologous proteins CHP1 and CHP2 (Di Sole et al., 2012). CHPs interact with several isoforms of sodium/proton exchangers (NHEs), and this interaction is required for the localization and function of NHE transporters on the plasma membrane (Pedersen and Counillon, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kolobynina et al., 2016; Di Sole et al., 2012; Pedersen and Counillon, 2019) that establish CHP3's identity and function.

claim: CHP3 interacts with calcineurin A.
source: Besides NHEs, CHP3 interacts with calcineurin A (Gutierrez-Ford et al., 2003), subunit 4 of COP9 signalosome (Levay and Slepak, 2014) and glycogen synthase kinase 3 (GSK3) (Kobayashi et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gutierrez-Ford et al., 2003.

claim: CHP3 interacts with subunit 4 of COP9 signalosome.
source: Besides NHEs, CHP3 interacts with calcineurin A (Gutierrez-Ford et al., 2003), subunit 4 of COP9 signalosome (Levay and Slepak, 2014) and glycogen synthase kinase 3 (GSK3) (Kobayashi et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Levay and Slepak, 2014.

claim: CHP3 interacts with glycogen synthase kinase 3 (GSK3).
source: Besides NHEs, CHP3 interacts with calcineurin A (Gutierrez-Ford et al., 2003), subunit 4 of COP9 signalosome (Levay and Slepak, 2014) and glycogen synthase kinase 3 (GSK3) (Kobayashi et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kobayashi et al., 2015.

claim: CHP3 expression level correlates with the progression, metastasis, and invasiveness of gastric, renal, and colorectal cancers.
source: Recent studies revealed that the CHP3 expression level correlates with the progression, metastasis, and invasiveness of gastric, renal, and colorectal cancers (Kang et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2018; Luo et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Kang et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2018; Luo et al., 2019).

claim: Genome-wide association studies in combination with neuroimaging identified CHP3 as a key regulator of neurogenesis for hippocampal volume formation.
source: In addition, genome-wide association studies in combination with neuroimaging identified CHP3 as a key regulator of neurogenesis for hippocampal volume formation (Dannlowski et al., 2015; Horgusluoglu-Moloch et al., 2019; Stein et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies (Dannlowski et al., 2015; Horgusluoglu-Moloch et al., 2019; Stein et al., 2012).

claim: CHP3 counteracts cardiac hypertrophy via regulation of GSK3 and calcineurin activities.
source: Via regulation of GSK3 and calcineurin activities, it seems to counteract cardiac hypertrophy (Kobayashi et al., 2015; Viereck et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kobayashi et al., 2015 and Viereck et al., 2020.

claim: All three CHPs undergo conformational changes upon Ca2+ binding.
source: All three CHPs were shown to undergo conformational changes upon Ca2+ binding (Gutierrez-Ford et al., 2003; Liang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gutierrez-Ford et al., 2003 and Liang et al., 2020.

claim: CHP3 has a lower affinity for Ca2+ (0.8 µM) in comparison to CHP1 and CHP2 (KD values below 100 nM).
source: Notably, CHP3 has a lower affinity for Ca2+ (0.8 µM) (Gutierrez-Ford et al., 2003) in comparison to CHP1 and CHP2 (KD values below 100 nM) (Li et al., 2011; Pang et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies that measured Ca2+ binding affinities (Gutierrez-Ford et al., 2003; Li et al., 2011; Pang et al., 2004).

claim: Ca2+-binding affinities of CHP1 and CHP2 strongly increased (45- and 42-fold, respectively) upon binding of the NHE1 target peptide.
source: Further, Ca2+-binding affinities of CHP1 and CHP2 strongly increased (45- and 42-fold, respectively) upon binding of the NHE1 target peptide (Li et al., 2011; Pang et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2011 and Pang et al., 2004.

claim: CHP3 binds Mg2+ with a low affinity (KD = 73 µM) in the absence of Ca2+.
source: CHP3 binds also Mg2+ with a low affinity (KD = 73 µM) in the absence of Ca2+.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and is based on previously published data as indicated by the context.

claim: The presence of 1 mM Mg2+ reduces the affinity of CHP3 for Ca2+ from 0.8 to 3.5 µM.
source: The presence of 1 mM Mg2+ reduces the affinity for Ca2+ from 0.8 to 3.5 µM, indicating a direct competition between Ca2+ and Mg2+ for the EF-3 binding site (Gutierrez-Ford et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gutierrez-Ford et al., 2003.

claim: CHP3 harbors an N-terminal myristoylation site similar to other EFCaBPs such as recoverin and calcineurin B.
source: In addition, CHP3 harbors an N-terminal myristoylation site similar to other EFCaBPs such as recoverin and calcineurin B (Gutierrez-Ford et al., 2003; Zaun et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gutierrez-Ford et al., 2003 and Zaun et al., 2012.

claim: Myristoylated CHP1 binds to microsomal membranes in a Ca2+-dependent manner indicating the presence of a Ca2+-myristoyl switch.
source: Myristoylated CHP1 binds to microsomal membranes in a Ca2+-dependent manner indicating the presence of a Ca2+-myristoyl switch (Andrade et al., 2004), whereas binding of myristoylated CHP3 to lipid membranes has not been reported so far.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Andrade et al., 2004.

claim: Co-expression of NHE1 with CHP3 that lacks myristoylation and/or Ca2+-binding sites significantly reduced the half-life at the cell surface and the activity of this transporter.
source: Co-expression of NHE1 with CHP3 that lacks myristoylation and/or Ca2+-binding sites significantly reduced the half-life at the cell surface and the activity of this transporter (Zaun et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zaun et al., 2012.

claim: CHP3 binds at 1:1 ratio to the CHP-binding region of human NHE1 (CBD) with high affinity in the presence of Mg2+.
source: We previously demonstrated that CHP3 binds at 1:1 ratio to the CHP-binding region of human NHE1 (CBD) with high affinity in the presence of Mg2+ (Fuchs et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fuchs et al., 2018.

claim: Addition of Ca2+ increased the amount of the CHP3-myc and NHE1-HA complex formed as shown by co-immunoprecipitation.
source: At the same time, it was shown by co-immunoprecipitation of CHP3-myc and NHE1-HA that addition of Ca2+ increased the amount of the complex formed (Zaun et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zaun et al., 2012.

claim: Ca2+ and N-terminal myristoylation independently regulate the conformation of CHP3 and its interaction with NHE1.
source: Here, we show that Ca2+ and N-terminal myristoylation independently regulate the conformation of CHP3 and its interaction with NHE1 providing the molecular basis for regulation of CHP3 function.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Surface exposure of the myristoyl moiety in CHP3 was triggered by target peptide binding as probed by interaction with liposomes.
source: This excludes a Ca2+-myristoyl switch in CHP3, instead, surface exposure of the myristoyl moiety was triggered by target peptide binding as probed by interaction with liposomes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data on liposome binding.

claim: Pure untagged CHP3 and myristoylated CHP3 (mCHP3) were obtained using Ca2+-dependent hydrophobic interaction chromatography (HIC) for purification.
source: Here, we produced untagged CHP3 and mCHP3, the latter by co-expression with human N-myristoyltransferase 1, and used Ca2+-dependent hydrophobic interaction chromatography (HIC) for purification.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental method used in this study.

claim: Combining HIC and gel filtration, pure untagged proteins were obtained with an average yield of 9 mg/l of expression culture.
source: Combining HIC and gel filtration, we obtained pure untagged proteins, as shown by sodium dodecyl sulfate–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS–PAGE) analysis (Figure 1A) with an average yield of 9 mg/l of expression culture.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and reference to Figure 1A showing SDS-PAGE analysis.

claim: The measured mass of mCHP3 was increased by ~211 Da in comparison to CHP3, which is in agreement with the covalent attachment of one myristoyl group (Mr = 210 Da).
source: The measured mass of mCHP3 was increased by ~211 Da (Figure 1B, bottom) in comparison to CHP3 (Figure 1B, top), which is in agreement with the covalent attachment of one myristoyl group (Mr = 210 Da).
evidence: The claim is supported by native MS data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Native MS analysis of three independently produced and purified samples confirmed reproducible complete myristoylation of recombinant CHP3.
source: Native MS analysis of three independently produced and purified samples confirmed reproducible complete myristoylation of recombinant CHP3.
evidence: The claim is supported by native MS experimental data.

claim: The ion mobility arrival time was shorter for mCHP3 indicating a more compact shape of mCHP3 compared to CHP3.
source: Interestingly, the ion mobility arrival time was shorter for mCHP3 (Figure 1C) indicating a more compact shape of mCHP3 compared to CHP3.
evidence: The claim is supported by ion mobility data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The molecular masses of both CHP3 and mCHP3 were shifted by ~40 Da after addition of Ca2+, which corresponds to the binding of a single Ca2+ ion.
source: The molecular masses of both proteins were shifted by ~40 Da (Figure 1B), which corresponds to the binding of a single Ca2+ ion and, thus, documents that both recombinant CHP3 and mCHP3 are functional in respect to Ca2+ binding and confirms the presence of one Ca2+-binding site (Gutierrez-Ford et al., 2003; Perera et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by native MS data shown in Figure 1B and citations to previous studies.

claim: After Ca2+ addition, the fluorescence intensity increased by 30% and 40% for CHP3 and mCHP3, respectively, reflecting an increase in hydrophobicity.
source: After Ca2+ addition, the fluorescence intensity increased by 30% and 40% for CHP3 and mCHP3, respectively, reflecting an increase in hydrophobicity (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by FPH assay data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Ca2+ removal by EGTA reduced the fluorescence to the initial level, indicating the reversibility of Ca2+ binding and of the respective conformational changes.
source: Ca2+ removal by EGTA reduced the fluorescence to the initial level, indicating the reversibility of Ca2+ binding and of the respective conformational changes.
evidence: The claim is supported by FPH assay data.

claim: The N-terminal myristoylation did not affect the conformational changes of CHP3.
source: Interestingly, the N-terminal myristoylation did not affect the conformational changes of CHP3.
evidence: The claim is supported by FPH assay data comparing CHP3 and mCHP3.

claim: Ca2+ induced similar changes of non-myristoylated recoverin as of CHP3 in the FPH assay, whereas hydrophobicity of the myristoylated protein increased much stronger (about 3.5-fold) in response to Ca2+ binding.
source: Ca2+ induced similar changes of non-myristoylated recoverin as of CHP3 in the FPH assay, whereas hydrophobicity of the myristoylated protein increased much stronger (about 3.5-fold) in response to Ca2+ binding, which most likely resulted from the exposure of the myristic group.
evidence: The claim is supported by FPH assay data on recoverin as a control protein.

claim: Ca2+ addition decreased the intrinsic fluorescence of CHP3 reflecting conformational changes accompanied with changes in the local environment of Trp191 in the hydrophobic pocket.
source: Ca2+ addition decreased the intrinsic fluorescence of CHP3 (Figure 2B) reflecting conformational changes accompanied with changes in the local environment of Trp191 in the hydrophobic pocket.
evidence: The claim is supported by intrinsic tryptophan fluorescence data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The EC50 value for binding of Ca2+ to CHP3 in the presence of Mg2+ is 161.1 [112.6; 233.8] μM.
source: We determined Ca2+ EC50 values performing a global fit for all data. The difference between EC50's obtained for CHP3 (161.1 [112.6; 233.8] μM; Figure 2D) and mCHP3 (152.6 [113.7; 209.7] µM; Figure 2E) is insignificant, indicating that myristoylation does not affect the Ca2+-binding properties of CHP3.
evidence: The claim is supported by FPH assay data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The EC50 value for binding of Ca2+ to mCHP3 in the presence of Mg2+ is 152.6 [113.7; 209.7] µM.
source: We determined Ca2+ EC50 values performing a global fit for all data. The difference between EC50's obtained for CHP3 (161.1 [112.6; 233.8] μM; Figure 2D) and mCHP3 (152.6 [113.7; 209.7] µM; Figure 2E) is insignificant, indicating that myristoylation does not affect the Ca2+-binding properties of CHP3.
evidence: The claim is supported by FPH assay data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Myristoylation does not affect the Ca2+-binding properties of CHP3.
source: The difference between EC50's obtained for CHP3 (161.1 [112.6; 233.8] μM; Figure 2D) and mCHP3 (152.6 [113.7; 209.7] µM; Figure 2E) is insignificant, indicating that myristoylation does not affect the Ca2+-binding properties of CHP3.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of EC50 values from FPH assay data.

claim: Free CHP3 had the highest thermal stability in the Mg2+-bound state (Tmapp 70.1 ± 0.3°C).
source: Free CHP3 had the highest thermal stability in the Mg2+-bound state (Tmapp 70.1 ± 0.3°C), and Ca2+ binding reduced the melting point to 66.9 ± 0.2°C (CHP3 in Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by nanoDSF data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Ca2+ binding reduced the melting point of CHP3 to 66.9 ± 0.2°C.
source: Free CHP3 had the highest thermal stability in the Mg2+-bound state (Tmapp 70.1 ± 0.3°C), and Ca2+ binding reduced the melting point to 66.9 ± 0.2°C (CHP3 in Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by nanoDSF data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Binding of the target peptide CBD strongly increased the thermal stability for the Ca2+-bound and apo-states of CHP3.
source: Notably, binding of the target peptide CBD strongly increased the thermal stability for the Ca2+-bound and apo-states (compare CHP3 and CHP3:CBD in Figure 3), with about 12°C in the presence of Ca2+, 13°C in the presence of Ca2+ plus Mg2+ and about 11°C for the apo-state.
evidence: The claim is supported by nanoDSF data shown in Figure 3.

claim: CBD binding did not have any effect on the thermal stability of the Mg2+-bound state of CHP3.
source: Surprisingly, CBD binding did not have any effect on the thermal stability of the Mg2+-bound state.
evidence: The claim is supported by nanoDSF data.

claim: The N-terminal myristoylation decreased the Tmapp of CHP3 in all states to the same degree (9.8°C for Mg2+-bound and 10.6°C for Ca2+-bound states, 10.9°C in the presence of both ions, 4.5°C for the already destabilized apo-state).
source: The N-terminal myristoylation decreased the Tmapp of CHP3 in all states to the same degree (9.8°C for Mg2+-bound and 10.6°C for Ca2+-bound states, 10.9°C in the presence of both ions, 4.5°C for the already destabilized apo-state) (compare CHP3 and mCHP3 in Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by nanoDSF data shown in Figure 3.

claim: CHP3 was readily proteolysed by trypsin with nearly one half of the protein already degraded after 5 min and almost no full-length protein remained after 60-min incubation.
source: CHP3 was readily proteolysed by trypsin with nearly one half of the protein already degraded after 5 min and almost no full-length protein remained after 60-min incubation (Figure 4A, top, FL).
evidence: The claim is supported by limited proteolysis data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Fragment 1 has a mass of 17.92 kDa corresponding to residues 2–155 of CHP3 lacking the C-terminal part.
source: Fragment 1 has a mass of 17.92 kDa corresponding to residues 2–155 of CHP3 (UniProtID Q96BS2-1) lacking the C-terminal part (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by MS analysis of proteolytic fragments.

claim: Fragment 2 has a mass of 9.63 kDa and includes residues 74–155.
source: Fragment 2 has a mass of 9.63 kDa and includes residues 74–155. Thus, it derived from a cleavage of fragment 1 within the predicted EF-2 (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by MS analysis of proteolytic fragments.

claim: Target peptide binding nearly completely prevented the trypsin cleavage of CHP3.
source: Target peptide binding nearly completely prevented the trypsin cleavage, and the intensity of the full-length CHP3 band was only slightly reduced even after 60-min incubation (Figure 4A, bottom).
evidence: The claim is supported by limited proteolysis data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In the presence of Ca2+, the cleavage of fragment 1 was more pronounced and was accompanied with an increase of fragment 2.
source: Fragment 1 appeared already after 5 min and degraded further over time (Figure 4B, 1), its cleavage was more pronounced in the presence of Ca2+ and was accompanied with an increase of fragment 2 (Figure 4B, 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by limited proteolysis data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: N-terminal myristoylation did not affect the proteolytic stability of the full-length protein, whereas it slightly reduced the stability of fragment 1 in all states.
source: N-terminal myristoylation did not affect the proteolytic stability of the full-length protein, whereas it slightly reduced the stability of fragment 1 in all states.
evidence: The claim is supported by limited proteolysis data.

claim: The complex formation with CBD drastically increased the proteolytic stability of both CHP3 and mCHP3, as nearly no degradation occurred under all analysed experimental conditions.
source: The complex formation with CBD drastically increased the proteolytic stability of both CHP3 and mCHP3, as nearly no degradation occurred under all analysed experimental conditions (Figure 4B, CHP3:CBD and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by limited proteolysis data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The dissociation constant (KD) for CHP3:CBD in the Ca2+-bound state is 3.1 [2.8; 3.4] nM.
source: Namely, Ca2+ binding increased affinities for CBD of both non-myristoylated (CHP3:CBD, KD = 3.1 [2.8; 3.4] nM) and myristoylated CHP3 (mCHP3:CBD, KD = 5.6 [5.1; 6.2] nM) by about fivefold as compared to the Mg2+-bound state (CHP3:CBD, KD = 14.6 [12.5; 16.9] nM; mCHP3:CBD, KD = 28.2 [26.6; 29.8] nM) (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by MST data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The dissociation constant (KD) for mCHP3:CBD in the Ca2+-bound state is 5.6 [5.1; 6.2] nM.
source: Namely, Ca2+ binding increased affinities for CBD of both non-myristoylated (CHP3:CBD, KD = 3.1 [2.8; 3.4] nM) and myristoylated CHP3 (mCHP3:CBD, KD = 5.6 [5.1; 6.2] nM) by about fivefold as compared to the Mg2+-bound state (CHP3:CBD, KD = 14.6 [12.5; 16.9] nM; mCHP3:CBD, KD = 28.2 [26.6; 29.8] nM) (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by MST data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The dissociation constant (KD) for CHP3:CBD in the Mg2+-bound state is 14.6 [12.5; 16.9] nM.
source: Namely, Ca2+ binding increased affinities for CBD of both non-myristoylated (CHP3:CBD, KD = 3.1 [2.8; 3.4] nM) and myristoylated CHP3 (mCHP3:CBD, KD = 5.6 [5.1; 6.2] nM) by about fivefold as compared to the Mg2+-bound state (CHP3:CBD, KD = 14.6 [12.5; 16.9] nM; mCHP3:CBD, KD = 28.2 [26.6; 29.8] nM) (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by MST data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The dissociation constant (KD) for mCHP3:CBD in the Mg2+-bound state is 28.2 [26.6; 29.8] nM.
source: Namely, Ca2+ binding increased affinities for CBD of both non-myristoylated (CHP3:CBD, KD = 3.1 [2.8; 3.4] nM) and myristoylated CHP3 (mCHP3:CBD, KD = 5.6 [5.1; 6.2] nM) by about fivefold as compared to the Mg2+-bound state (CHP3:CBD, KD = 14.6 [12.5; 16.9] nM; mCHP3:CBD, KD = 28.2 [26.6; 29.8] nM) (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by MST data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Ca2+ binding increased affinities for CBD of both non-myristoylated and myristoylated CHP3 by about fivefold as compared to the Mg2+-bound state.
source: Namely, Ca2+ binding increased affinities for CBD of both non-myristoylated (CHP3:CBD, KD = 3.1 [2.8; 3.4] nM) and myristoylated CHP3 (mCHP3:CBD, KD = 5.6 [5.1; 6.2] nM) by about fivefold as compared to the Mg2+-bound state (CHP3:CBD, KD = 14.6 [12.5; 16.9] nM; mCHP3:CBD, KD = 28.2 [26.6; 29.8] nM) (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by MST data shown in Figure 5.

claim: For both Ca2+- and Mg2+-bound states, myristoylation decreased the affinity of CHP3 for CBD twofold.
source: In turn, for both Ca2+- and Mg2+-bound states, myristoylation decreased the affinity twofold (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by MST data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Non-myristoylated recoverin (Rec) only weakly interacted with liposomes in both Mg2+- and Ca2+-bound states.
source: In line with previous studies (Zozulya and Stryer, 1992), non-myristoylated recoverin (Rec) only weakly interacted with liposomes in both Mg2+- and Ca2+-bound states, whereas the interaction of myristoylated protein (mRec) increased about fourfold upon Ca2+ addition (Figure 6A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by liposome co-sedimentation assay data shown in Figure 6A, B and citation to Zozulya and Stryer, 1992.

claim: The interaction of myristoylated recoverin (mRec) with liposomes increased about fourfold upon Ca2+ addition.
source: In line with previous studies (Zozulya and Stryer, 1992), non-myristoylated recoverin (Rec) only weakly interacted with liposomes in both Mg2+- and Ca2+-bound states, whereas the interaction of myristoylated protein (mRec) increased about fourfold upon Ca2+ addition (Figure 6A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by liposome co-sedimentation assay data shown in Figure 6A, B and citation to Zozulya and Stryer, 1992.

claim: In the Mg2+-bound state, CHP3 interacted weakly with liposomes similar to recoverin.
source: In the Mg2+-bound state, CHP3 interacted weakly with liposomes similar to recoverin, only a small protein amount co-sedimented with liposomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by liposome co-sedimentation assay data.

claim: Ca2+ addition increased the binding of non-myristoylated CHP3 to liposomes about 2.5 times.
source: In contrast to recoverin, Ca2+ addition increased the binding of non-myristoylated CHP3 (about 2.5 times) to liposomes, whereas myristoylation did not further increase this binding (Figure 6A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by liposome co-sedimentation assay data shown in Figure 6A, B.

claim: Myristoylation did not further increase the binding of CHP3 to liposomes in the presence of Ca2+.
source: In contrast to recoverin, Ca2+ addition increased the binding of non-myristoylated CHP3 (about 2.5 times) to liposomes, whereas myristoylation did not further increase this binding (Figure 6A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by liposome co-sedimentation assay data shown in Figure 6A, B.

claim: In both the absence and the presence of Ca2+, only a small amount of the CHP3:CBD complex was associated with liposomes.
source: Interestingly, the binding of the target peptide CBD substantially changed the interaction of CHP3 with liposomes. In both the absence and the presence of Ca2+, only a small amount of the CHP3:CBD complex was associated with liposomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by liposome co-sedimentation assay data.

claim: CHP3 myristoylation increased the binding of CHP3:CBD complex to liposomes about fourfold.
source: However, CHP3 myristoylation increased the binding in both conditions about fourfold (Figure 6A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by liposome co-sedimentation assay data shown in Figure 6A, B.

claim: LC–MS/MS analysis identified the vast majority of MS-accessible CHP3 peptides, but only the myristoylated form of the N-terminal peptide in three different preparations from mouse tissues.
source: In three different preparations, namely (1) size fractionated complexes from mouse brain membranes (Figure 6C), (2) integral membrane proteins isolated from mouse platelets (i.e. after carbonate extraction, Figure 6—figure supplement 1), and (3) anti-NHE1-affinity purification from solubilized mouse brain membranes (data not shown) we identified the vast majority of MS-accessible CHP3 peptides, but only the myristoylated form of the N-terminal peptide.
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Myristoylated CHP3 is both NHE1 associated and membrane anchored in vivo.
source: Together, this suggests that myristoylated CHP3 is both NHE1 associated and membrane anchored in agreement with a target-induced exposure and membrane integration of the N-terminal myristoyl moiety.
evidence: The claim is inferred from LC-MS/MS data showing myristoylated CHP3 in membrane fractions and NHE1-associated complexes.

claim: CHP3 undergoes reversible Ca2+-induced conformational changes as typical for a Ca2+ sensor protein.
source: Combining the data of the FPH assay and of the intrinsic tryptophan fluorescence, we conclude that CHP3 undergoes reversible Ca2+-induced conformational changes as typical for a Ca2+ sensor protein.
evidence: The claim is supported by FPH assay and intrinsic fluorescence data.

claim: The hydrophobic target-binding pocket of CHP3 is occluded in the Mg2+-bound state (closed conformation), and becomes exposed to the environment upon Ca2+ binding (open conformation).
source: The hydrophobic target-binding pocket of CHP3 is occluded in the Mg2+-bound state (closed conformation), and becomes exposed to the environment upon Ca2+ binding (open conformation).
evidence: The claim is inferred from FPH assay and intrinsic fluorescence data showing increased hydrophobicity upon Ca2+ binding.

claim: Mg2+ binding is important to stabilize the closed conformation of target-free protein in the cell at resting Ca2+ level.
source: As we observed that CHP3 is not stable in the apo-state, we conclude that Mg2+ binding is important to stabilize the closed conformation of target-free protein in the cell at resting Ca2+ level.
evidence: The claim is inferred from thermal stability data showing destabilization in the apo-state.

claim: Replacement of Mg2+ with Ca2+ at EF-3 (C-lobe) lowered the thermal stability of CHP3 and mCHP3 and enhanced proteolytic cleavage in EF-2 (N-lobe) suggesting an increase in local flexibility.
source: Further, replacement of Mg2+ with Ca2+ at EF-3 (C-lobe) lowered the thermal stability of CHP3 and mCHP3 and enhanced proteolytic cleavage in EF-2 (N-lobe) suggesting an increase in local flexibility.
evidence: The claim is supported by thermal stability and limited proteolysis data.

claim: Ca2+-induced conformational changes involve not only the C-lobe of CHP3 but also its N-lobe.
source: Thus, Ca2+-induced conformational changes involve not only the C-lobe of CHP3 but also its N-lobe.
evidence: The claim is inferred from proteolysis data showing enhanced cleavage in EF-2 (N-lobe) upon Ca2+ binding.

claim: The Ca2+-induced open conformation with lower thermal stability and increased local flexibility appears to provide the molecular basis for CHP3 to interact more readily with its target(s).
source: The Ca2+-induced open conformation with lower thermal stability and increased local flexibility appears to provide the molecular basis for CHP3 to interact more readily with its target(s) (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is inferred from thermal stability, proteolysis, and binding affinity data.

claim: The binding of the target peptide resulted in a drastic increase of CHP3 thermal and proteolytic stabilities.
source: Firstly, the binding of the target peptide resulted in a drastic increase of CHP3 thermal and proteolytic stabilities.
evidence: The claim is supported by thermal stability and limited proteolysis data.

claim: The thermal stability of CHP3:CBD complex increased only in the presence of Ca2+, whereas for the Mg2+-bound state it remained unchanged.
source: However, the thermal stability increased only in the presence of Ca2+, whereas for the Mg2+-bound state it remained unchanged.
evidence: The claim is supported by nanoDSF data.

claim: The affinity of the Ca2+-bound CHP3 for CBD was about five times higher than the Mg2+-bound state.
source: The quantitative analysis with MST showed that the affinity of the Ca2+-bound state was about five times higher, clearly indicating that Ca2+ controls CHP3 function.
evidence: The claim is supported by MST data.

claim: The data exclude the proposed Ca2+-myristoyl switch for CHP3.
source: Our data indicate an independent regulation of CHP3 by Ca2+ binding and myristoylation, and contradict the presence of a Ca2+-myristoyl switch.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including FPH assay, thermal stability, and liposome binding data.

claim: Although Ca2+ addition strongly increased the CHP3 association with POPC/POPS liposomes, the effect was the same for both myristoylated and non-myristoylated proteins.
source: Although Ca2+ addition strongly increased the CHP3 association with POPC/POPS liposomes, the effect was the same for both myristoylated and non-myristoylated proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by liposome co-sedimentation assay data.

claim: The target peptide competes with the myristoyl moiety for binding in the hydrophobic pocket and by this way shifts the conformational equilibrium of CHP3, resulting in the exposure of the myristoyl moiety to the environment.
source: We propose that the target peptide competes with the myristoyl moiety for binding in the hydrophobic pocket and by this way shifts the conformational equilibrium of CHP3, resulting in the exposure of the myristoyl moiety to the environment (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is a proposed mechanism based on liposome binding data and MST data showing reduced affinity of mCHP3 for CBD.

claim: The myristoyl moiety binds most likely weakly or transiently to the target-binding pocket.
source: As the effect on affinity is small, the myristoyl moiety binds most likely weakly or transiently to the target-binding pocket.
evidence: The claim is inferred from MST data showing a small decrease in affinity of mCHP3 for CBD.

claim: The target-myristoyl switch is the canonical mechanism to anchor the regulatory domain of NHE1 to the plasma membrane.
source: We suggest that the target-myristoyl switch is the canonical mechanism to anchor the regulatory domain of NHE1 to the plasma membrane, which appears to be the molecular basis for an increase of NHE1 surface stability by CHP3.
evidence: The claim is a proposed mechanism based on experimental data and inference.

claim: Ca2+ binding to CHP3 can affect NHE1:CHP3 interaction in two ways: Ca2+ directly increases the binding affinity of CHP3 for NHE1, and indirectly increases the probability to interact with NHE1 via enhanced association of free CHP3 with lipid membranes.
source: As the second mode of regulation, Ca2+ binding to CHP3 can affect NHE1:CHP3 interaction in two ways. Ca2+ directly increases the binding affinity of CHP3 for NHE1, and indirectly increases the probability to interact with NHE1 via enhanced association of free CHP3 with lipid membranes.
evidence: The claim is a proposed mechanism based on MST and liposome binding data.

claim: Recombinant myristoylated CHP3 was produced by co-expression with human N-myristoyltransferase 1.
source: Here, we produced untagged CHP3 and mCHP3, the latter by co-expression with human N-myristoyltransferase 1, and used Ca2+-dependent hydrophobic interaction chromatography (HIC) for purification.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental method used in this study.

claim: Both CHP3 and mCHP3 form only monomers under reducing conditions in the presence of 2 mM TCEP.
source: Both proteins form only monomers under reducing conditions in the presence of 2 mM TCEP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by gel filtration data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The single tryptophan residue (Trp191) is located in CHP3's hydrophobic target-binding pocket at the protein surface.
source: According to the 3D model of CHP3 predicted with AlphaFold2.0 (Varadi et al., 2022), the single tryptophan residue (Trp191) is located in CHP3's hydrophobic target-binding pocket at the protein surface (Figure 2C) in line with the measured emission maxima of CHP3 and mCHP3 of ~330 nm (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on the AlphaFold2.0 model and supported by intrinsic fluorescence data.

claim: CHP3 has one active EF-hand only, which is EF-3.
source: Noteworthy, both fragments still contain the single functional EF-hand of CHP3 (EF-3).
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis and previous studies.

claim: EF-2 and EF-4 of CHP3 have 9-residue insertions, which disrupt the canonical Ca2+-coordinating loop.
source: CHP3 has a 9-amino acid long insertion in that position as compared to CHP1 and CHP2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: EF-1 of CHP3 lacks the conservative negatively charged residues important for Ca2+ coordination.
source: EF-1 of CHP3 lacks the conservative negatively charged residues important for Ca2+ coordination (positions X, Y and –Z, respective CHP3 residues are S36, G37, and N46).
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The AlphaFold2.0 model of CHP3 closely resembles the structures of CHP1 and CHP2 in complex with CBD.
source: This model closely resembles the structures of CHP1 and CHP2 in complex with CBD (Ammar et al., 2006; Mishima et al., 2007), of CHP1 in complex with full-length NHE1 (Dong et al., 2021) and of CHP1 with an artificial C-terminal helix bound in the target-binding pocket (Kennedy et al., 1996), that is structures of target-bound CHPs.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of the AlphaFold2.0 model with published structures.

claim: Both major cleavage sites are highly unlikely to be covered by CBD in the complex, as they are facing away from the target-binding pocket.
source: Both major cleavage sites are highly unlikely to be covered by CBD in the complex, as they are facing away from the target-binding pocket (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the AlphaFold2.0 model shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The drastic changes in the proteolytic stability indicate reduced flexibility in EF-2 and EF-4, which could be caused by structural rearrangements of CHP3 upon target peptide binding.
source: Thus, the drastic changes in the proteolytic stability indicate reduced flexibility in EF-2 and EF-4, which could be caused by structural rearrangements of CHP3 upon target peptide binding.
evidence: The claim is inferred from limited proteolysis data.

claim: CHP3 binds to NHE1 with nanomolar affinity in both open and closed conformation and independently of its modification.
source: Hence, CHP3 binds to NHE1 with nanomolar affinity in both open and closed conformation and independently of its modification, however, Ca2+ binding and myristoylation modulates the affinity.
evidence: The claim is supported by MST data.

claim: Ca2+ binding and myristoylation modulate the affinity of CHP3 for NHE1.
source: Hence, CHP3 binds to NHE1 with nanomolar affinity in both open and closed conformation and independently of its modification, however, Ca2+ binding and myristoylation modulates the affinity.
evidence: The claim is supported by MST data.

claim: The effects of Ca2+ and myristoylation on CHP3:CBD interaction are independent.
source: Comparison of the resulting KD values showed that the effects of Ca2+ binding and myristoylation on CHP3:CBD interaction are independent.
evidence: The claim is supported by MST data showing additive effects.

claim: The myristic moiety is located in the protein core of target-free CHP3 and is not accessible to lipid membranes in the presence of Ca2+.
source: The myristic moiety is located in the protein core of target-free CHP3 and is not accessible to lipid membranes in the presence of Ca2+.
evidence: The claim is inferred from liposome binding data showing no difference between CHP3 and mCHP3 in Ca2+ condition.

claim: Target peptide binding causes conformational rearrangements with displacement of the myristic moiety from the protein core to the environment, which leads in consequence to an increased association of CHP3 and its target to lipid membranes.
source: Most likely, other protein regions are involved in membrane binding in this case. Target peptide binding causes conformational rearrangements with displacement of the myristic moiety from the protein core to the environment, which leads in consequence to an increased association of CHP3 and its target to lipid membranes.
evidence: The claim is a proposed mechanism based on liposome binding data.

claim: CHP3 should be present in the Mg2+-bound state in a cell at basal Ca2+ concentration, ready to respond to Ca2+ signals.
source: Thus, CHP3 should be present in the Mg2+-bound state in a cell at basal Ca2+ concentration, ready to respond to Ca2+ signals, yet, the exact mechanism is not fully described.
evidence: The claim is inferred from Ca2+ and Mg2+ binding affinities and cellular ion concentrations.

claim: CHP3 may respond to Ca2+ signals with conformational changes when the intracellular Ca2+ concentration elevates from 100 nM to 1 µM or higher.
source: CHP3 may thus respond to Ca2+ signals with conformational changes when the intracellular Ca2+ concentration elevates from 100 nM to 1 µM or higher (Roderick and Cook, 2008).
evidence: The claim is inferred from Ca2+ binding affinity and cellular Ca2+ concentrations, supported by citation.

claim: Ca2+-induced conformational changes are characteristic for Ca2+ sensor proteins such as calmodulin (CaM) and calcineurin B.
source: Ca2+-induced conformational changes are characteristic for Ca2+ sensor proteins such as calmodulin (CaM) and calcineurin B (Creamer, 2020; Nelson and Chazin, 1998).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: At the resting Ca2+ level, Ca2+ sensor proteins adopt a closed conformation, in which the hydrophobic target-binding pocket is occluded.
source: At the resting Ca2+ level, they adopt a closed conformation, in which the hydrophobic target-binding pocket is occluded.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Ca2+ sensor proteins.

claim: Upon a rise of the intracellular Ca2+ concentration, Ca2+ binding to EF-hand(s) causes an opening of the hydrophobic pocket providing the structural basis for the transmission of Ca2+ signals.
source: Upon a rise of the intracellular Ca2+ concentration, Ca2+ binding to EF-hand(s) causes an opening of this pocket providing the structural basis for the transmission of Ca2+ signals (Nelson and Chazin, 1998).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: This opening often triggers the binding of EFCaBPs to their target proteins.
source: This opening often triggers the binding of EFCaBPs to their target proteins (Burgoyne et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Ca2+-induced conformational changes of EFCaBPs such as calcineurin B or guanylyl cyclase activating proteins (GCAPs) stably associated with target proteins can affect the function of the latter.
source: In addition, Ca2+-induced conformational changes of EFCaBPs such as calcineurin B or guanylyl cyclase activating proteins (GCAPs) stably associated with target proteins can affect the function of the latter (Creamer, 2020; Lim et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Membrane binding via the myristoyl moiety is usually enforced with either a second lipidation site or clusters of positively charged and/or hydrophobic residues.
source: Membrane binding via the myristoyl moiety is usually enforced with either a second lipidation site or clusters of positively charged and/or hydrophobic residues (Yuan et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In many Ca2+ sensor proteins (for instance recoverin, neurocalcin, visinin-like proteins), the myristoyl group becomes accessible to lipid membranes after Ca2+ binding.
source: In many Ca2+ sensor proteins (for instance recoverin, neurocalcin, visinin-like proteins), the myristoyl group becomes accessible to lipid membranes after Ca2+ binding (Lim et al., 2014). This mechanism is called Ca2+-myristoyl switch.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Not all myristoylated EFCaBPs have a Ca2+-myristoyl switch.
source: However, not all myristoylated EFCaBPs have a Ca2+-myristoyl switch.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge.

claim: In the neuronal calcium sensor-1 (NCS-1) and in KChIP1, the myristoyl moiety becomes exposed in the presence of lipid membranes even at low Ca2+ concentration.
source: In the neuronal calcium sensor-1 (NCS-1) and in KChIP1, the myristoyl moiety becomes exposed in the presence of lipid membranes even at low Ca2+ concentration (Lim et al., 2014; McFerran et al., 1999; O'Callaghan and Burgoyne, 2004; O'Callaghan et al., 2003); and it is constantly hidden within the protein core in GCAPs (Lim et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The myristoyl group is constantly hidden within the protein core in GCAPs.
source: In the neuronal calcium sensor-1 (NCS-1) and in KChIP1, the myristoyl moiety becomes exposed in the presence of lipid membranes even at low Ca2+ concentration (Lim et al., 2014; McFerran et al., 1999; O'Callaghan and Burgoyne, 2004; O'Callaghan et al., 2003); and it is constantly hidden within the protein core in GCAPs (Lim et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: A Ca2+-myristoyl switch was proposed for CHP3 based on previous results.
source: Based on these results, the presence of a Ca2+-myristoyl switch for CHP3 was proposed (Gutierrez-Ford et al., 2003; Zaun et al., 2012), though the exposure of the myristoyl group in response to Ca2+ binding has not been shown experimentally.
evidence: The claim is based on citations to previous studies that proposed this mechanism.

claim: The exposure of the myristoyl group in response to Ca2+ binding has not been shown experimentally for CHP3 prior to this study.
source: Based on these results, the presence of a Ca2+-myristoyl switch for CHP3 was proposed (Gutierrez-Ford et al., 2003; Zaun et al., 2012), though the exposure of the myristoyl group in response to Ca2+ binding has not been shown experimentally.
evidence: The claim states a gap in previous research.
